column2: Courtyards of old blocks have a metal frame where people hang carpets to beat the dust out.
column4: Called 'trzepak' in Polish. Kids also used the frame as a goal or a climbing bar. Today it is mostly a relic, though many courtyards still have one.
column10: draft v3; theme: neighbours; fading; Wikipedia only (statements tagged citation needed); UA fit is a guess

column2: Every summer, the hot water in whole districts is switched off for a couple of weeks for pipe maintenance.
column4: Cities with district heating test and repair their mains in summer, so people boil kettles or shower at relatives'. Planned shutoffs are announced in advance.
column10: draft v3; theme: neighbours; source covers Kyiv only; PL fit not verified

column2: If you are out, the courier rings a neighbour, and you later collect your parcel from their door.
column4: Couriers try a neighbour first and tell you by message where the parcel ended up. It is why a short 'do you have my parcel?' knock is normal.
column10: draft v3; theme: neighbours; FR fit is a guess (gardien/neighbours often take parcels)

column2: Residents book the building's party hall for birthdays, and whoever asks first gets the date.
column4: 'Salão de festas' in Brazil, 'salón de eventos' in Mexico, 'clubhouse' in the US. House rules decide who may book, and holidays are often kept for the whole building.
column10: draft v3; theme: neighbours; MX and US fits are guesses

column2: On a local fiesta day, rockets go off before 6 a.m., and even irritated neighbours shrug it off as tradition.
column4: 'Cohetes' once called people to dawn services and processions. Expats often name them their top noise complaint; many locals dislike them but accept them.
column10: draft v3; theme: neighbours; religious roots; secular framing; regional (fiestas, esp. towns)

column2: The neighbourhood association can fine you for the wrong paint colour, a long lawn or bins left out.
column4: 'HOA' (homeowners association): rules cover mailboxes, parking, holiday decorations and snow clearing. Buyers are advised to read them before buying.
column10: draft v3; theme: neighbours

column2: A neighbour you have barely greeted may insist you come in for tea, and saying no once just starts the negotiation.
column4: A cup can turn into pastries, dinner and coffee over hours. Refusing is the opening bid, and the invitation is how people show interest.
column10: draft v3; theme: neighbours; close to tr-018 and ua-010; reviewer may drop; UA fit is a guess

column2: In flats, vacuuming or drilling in the early afternoon is frowned on, because those hours are for resting.
column4: 'Riposo pomeridiano': usually around 1 to 3 or 4 pm, set by city rules and the building's rulebook. Evenings and Sundays are quiet too.
column10: draft v3; theme: neighbours; hours vary by city and building

column2: The stairwell light switches itself off after a minute or so, and you press a glowing button to get it back.
column4: 'La minuterie': timers save power in shared areas. Many blocks across Europe have them; some newer ones use motion sensors instead.
column10: draft v3; theme: neighbours; fits guessed from general knowledge; source only confirms French timers

column2: Moving into a flat, you bring a plate of red-bean rice cake to the neighbours.
column4: 'Sirutteok': red beans were believed to drive out evil spirits. Today it is a friendly gesture, and rice cake shops say orders from movers have halved in ten years.
column10: draft v3; theme: neighbours; fading

column2: A voice from a speaker on the wall announces news to the whole apartment block, and you cannot switch it off.
column4: The management office broadcasts water cuts, lost-car notices and noise warnings. Large Korean complexes have long used these building announcements.
column10: draft v3; theme: neighbours; source is one expat blog; UA/PL/TR blocks may have similar systems

column2: Flowers for the hostess are handed over with the paper taken off first.
column4: Guides say odd number of stems, unwrapped, and no chrysanthemums. Florists add that odd numbers simply look better in a bouquet.
column10: draft v3; theme: gifts; UA fit from general knowledge; unwrapping rule varies by family

column2: Leaving your parents' home, you get a bag of jars: pickles, jam, soup, compote.
column4: Polish 'słoiki' (jars) is even a slang word for people who moved to the city from the provinces. Parents in many countries send grown-up kids off with home cooking.
column10: draft v3; theme: gifts; UA and KR fits from general knowledge; slang is derogatory, keep only in note

column2: Visiting a home with children, you bring a cake for the table and something sweet for the kids.
column4: A cake is a classic thank-you for the host, and children in the house may expect a sweet. Meals usually end with cake and tea or coffee.
column10: draft v3; theme: gifts; PL and TR fits are guesses; fairly generic

column2: Before the wedding, the bride's friends throw an afternoon party where everyone brings a pot, a plate or a kitchen tool.
column4: 'Chá de panela' (pot tea) in Brazil: each guest brings one kitchen item, often from the couple's list. The US bridal shower works much the same way.
column10: draft v3; theme: gifts; US fit is a guess; MX may have a similar custom

column2: Hosts hand every guest a small favour to take home, even at weddings and adult birthdays.
column4: 'Lembrancinha' in Brazil, 'bomboniera' in Italy, 'recuerdito' in Mexico. Weddings often use a small boxed sweet or keepsake with the couple's names.
column10: draft v3; theme: gifts; source is a vendor page; MX fit from general knowledge; US/NL/FR also have goodie bags for kids

column2: For weddings and baby showers, guests pick a gift from a list at a department store, which delivers it to the couple.
column4: In Mexico the 'mesa de regalos' at a big department store is a standard step; the list opens six months before the event. Registries work similarly in the US and Brazil.
column10: draft v3; theme: gifts; 2015 article; US/BR fits from general knowledge

column2: After a gift, you send a written thank-you note, even for a birthday or a graduation.
column4: Etiquette guides in the US advise a note within about a week. In French homes, a handwritten note the day after a dinner party is customary too.
column10: draft v3; theme: gifts; source is commercial; FR fit from annieandre.com guide

column2: Visitors to a newborn pin a small gold coin on the baby's blanket or clothes.
column4: 'Çeyrek altın' (quarter gold coin), often with a red ribbon; close relatives give half or full coins or a bracelet. The family keeps it as savings for the child.
column10: draft v3; theme: gifts; travel blog; Balkan/Middle East cultures outside the ten share it

column2: At weddings and graduations, guests go home with a little keepsake holding five sugared almonds.
column4: 'Bomboniera': five almonds for health, wealth, happiness, fertility and long life. White for weddings, red for graduations.
column10: draft v3; theme: gifts; colours are 'citation needed' on Wikipedia; BR fit is a guess

column2: Bringing a bottle to a dinner can read as doubting the host's choice, so it may stay corked that evening.
column4: French hosts pick wines to match the menu; a digestif, chocolates or pastries are safer. The rule is softening among younger hosts.
column10: draft v3; theme: gifts; softening; IT fit is a guess

column2: A gift is accepted with both hands and set aside unopened, not ripped open in front of the giver.
column4: Korean guides say gifts are never opened in front of the giver. The same advice appears for Poland and, in some guides, for Italy.
column10: draft v3; theme: gifts; UA guides say the opposite (opened right away); TR fit is a guess

column2: The housewarming party is nicknamed after the window ledge, where the first snacks were put.
column4: 'Parapetówka' comes from 'parapet' (window ledge). In Polish tradition the first party after moving in was once called 'setting in'.
column10: draft v3; theme: parties; etymology NOT verified; source only confirms housewarming customs; reviewer must check

column2: On their birthday, a child walks around the school with a small treat for every teacher.
column4: The 'traktatie' goes to classmates first. Most schools have a healthy-treat rule, and some now ban treats altogether.
column10: draft v3; theme: parties; fading in some schools

column2: At a friends' barbecue, each guest brings about a kilo of meat or chips in for the shopping.
column4: Group barbecues are cheap because costs are shared: about 300 g of meat per person is the rule of thumb.
column10: draft v3; theme: parties; fits guess: AR/UY not in the ten; US potluck is close

column2: Kids' birthdays invite the whole family and end with each guest taking home a bag of piñata candy.
column4: Mexican parties often have several piñatas and bouncy castles. Brazil sends guests home with a 'lembrancinha', and the US with a goodie bag.
column10: draft v3; theme: parties; overlaps mx-010/mx-012; BR and US fits from general knowledge

column2: A birthday starts with a song sung at dawn, sometimes with a band, to wake the person up.
column4: 'Las Mañanitas': sung at dawn to wake the person, and again around the cake. The singers swap in the birthday person's name.
column10: draft v3; theme: parties; Wikipedia does not mention the cake part; also sung on Mothers' Day

column2: After graduation, families host an afternoon open house where friends drop in, eat sheet cake and leave.
column4: Invitations give a window of hours rather than a start time. Many are backyard barbecues; some have grown into 'mini weddings' with DJs and food trucks.
column10: draft v3; theme: parties

column2: From about age 8, parents drop kids at a birthday party and come back to collect them at the end.
column4: Guides advise staying with under-5s. A French forum also reports parents leaving kids, with a flexible pick-up. Invitations should say which it is.
column10: draft v3; theme: parties; FR and NL fits uncertain; ages vary

column2: A group of women takes turns hosting an afternoon party, and everyone puts money or a gold coin in the pot for the host.
column4: A 'gün' (day) is part social club, part savings circle: the rotation continues until each member has had the pot. Korea has a similar savings circle, the 'gye'.
column10: draft v3; theme: parties; source blocked fetch (403) but search snippet matched; KR fit is a guess; fading among younger women

column2: On New Year's Eve, families stay in after a big dinner and play bingo for small prizes.
column4: 'Tombala' in Türkiye is a New Year's Eve classic; Italians play 'tombola' on Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve. Numbers are drawn from a bag.
column10: draft v3; theme: parties; IT game is strongly Christmas Eve; secular framing

column2: After Christmas Eve dinner, the whole family plays a bingo game, and the children shout when they win.
column4: 'Tombola': cards with numbers up to 90, prizes for two, three, four or five in a row. Grown-ups often let kids win. Türkiye's 'tombala' is similar.
column10: draft v3; theme: parties; religious holiday, secular custom: flag for review

column2: One evening in June, amateur and professional bands play free on street corners, and friends wander between them.
column4: 'La Fête de la musique' began in Paris in 1982, and about 120 countries now join. Italy's version is the 'Festa della Musica'.
column10: draft v3; theme: parties; public event rather than at home; many other countries take part

column2: After dinner with friends or colleagues, the group moves to a private room to sing, with a tambourine in hand.
column4: The 'noraebang' (singing room) is rented by the hour, so you sing just for your own group. It is often the second or later stop of the night out.
column10: draft v3; theme: parties; private-room karaoke also exists elsewhere in East Asia; round number varies
